turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Declan, come on in and sit yourself down. How have you been getting on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, I'm not too bad in myself, doctor, only the sugars are all over the shop and I was told to come in and talk it through properly.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. Start wherever you like, and take your time.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I do the finger prick most mornings, but I'm out the door at half five for the site, and the little booklet lives in the van, so when I try to read the numbers back they come out in a muddle.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Give me the muddle, then. What sort of figures have you been seeing?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The fasting one was one-eighty-something, I think, or it might have been one-sixty, the screen is tiny and I hadn't the glasses on me. After the breakfast it was two hundred and, I don't know, two-twenty, something around that. The machine beeps and I just put a squiggle in the book.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll not build a plan on a squiggle. How long have you had the diabetes?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's five years, well, actually, no, it'll be seven years this spring. I keep saying five and then I remember it was the same year Paudie, my brother, was told he had it too.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Seven years, and it's type 2, yes? Still on tablets and the insulin?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Type 2, yeah. Paudie has the type 2 as well, and he's on the metformin, only that's his prescription and his dose, not mine. I wouldn't want the two of us mixed up on the one page, we've the same surname and the chemist has done it before.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll keep Paudie out of your chart. Tell me what you take yourself.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformin, by mouth, five hundred milligrams twice a day, sorry, no, they put me up, it's a thousand milligrams twice a day, breakfast and the tea.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): A thousand milligrams twice a day, by mouth. Is there another tablet?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): There is. I nearly said glipizide, but that's wrong, it's gliclazide, eighty milligrams, one tablet in the morning with the breakfast. I've been on that a good while.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gliclazide eighty milligrams each morning. And the insulin, how are you using that?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Lantus, the insulin glargine, the long-acting one. I draw up eighteen units at night, into the tummy. That's what's written on a bit of tape on the pen.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse who took your details has twenty-four units on the chart, copied off the last letter she had. That's not eighteen.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty-four? No. The diabetes nurse in the hospital told me eighteen, and eighteen is what I draw up. She must have an old letter, I've never taken twenty-four.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the two of you have different doses written down, and I can't safely pick one today. We'll leave the number alone until the record is checked.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): That's fair. I'd rather nobody guessed it and I ended up on the floor.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): And do you actually get the injection in every night?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah now, on work days with the early shifts I come home wrecked and I skip it. Three nights a week, easy, and four if the job runs on. Weekends I never miss it, and I know well I shouldn't.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): So if I asked you how many doses you truly take in a week, you couldn't be sure.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I couldn't. Some weeks it's nearly the lot, some weeks it's half of them. It depends on the roster, and the roster changes.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other medicines in the house I should put on your list?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing of mine. My sister Maeve is on biotin for her hair, the chemist started her on it, but that's hers entirely. I don't take vitamins or any of that.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Maeve's biotin stays off your list. Any allergies, to medicines or anything else?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies. I've had penicillin in the past and I was grand with it, nothing came up.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): No known allergies, then. Apart from the numbers, how are you feeling day to day?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Washed out by the afternoon, doctor, a real tiredness, and I'm drinking water like nobody's business. Two big bottles on the site before I even think of the dinner.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has that thirst and the tiredness been going on?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): The thirst, maybe three months. The tiredness came along with it, the same sort of stretch. I blamed the job at first, the early starts and all.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any hypos? Shakes, sweats, a turn where you felt the sugar had gone too low?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No hypos. No shaking and no sweating like that, not this year anyway, and I'd know, I think.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the eyes? Any change in the sight?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit blurry in the evenings, watching the telly, the last couple of months. It's clearer in the morning once I'm up and going. I did have the eye screening, only I couldn't tell you when. Last year, or the year before, it's gone out of my head entirely.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): So we can't date that eye check. And the feet? Sores, pain, numbness, anything at all?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): The feet are grand. No sores, I check them in the shower, and there's no pain in them.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Even at night, nothing?

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, the toes tingle when I get into bed. Both feet, pins and needles, and it's been a few months. I didn't think that was worth mentioning when you said pain.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pins and needles counts. Let me have a look at the feet now.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, the boots are a terror, give me a second, there. I walk the site all day so the skin is fairly tough, but I do look.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): The skin is intact and I can't see any ulcer, on either foot. The pulses are present in both feet, and the filament sensation is reduced over the toes, both sides.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that serious? My father had circulation trouble, from the smoking, but he wasn't a diabetic, so I don't know if that runs in us.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can happen when the sugar stays high, the nerves in the toes getting a bit affected. That's what I'm thinking, not a finished diagnosis. Any chest pain, tightness, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain and no tightness. I'm not short of breath either, unless you count climbing the scaffolding, and that's the legs giving out, not the chest.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the waterworks? Up in the night, any burning?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm up once in the night to pass water, which I put down to all the drinking. No burning, nothing like that.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels behaving?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Bowels are grand, no change there at all. And I've lost a bit of weight, maybe half a stone since the summer, without trying. The work trousers are looser on me.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your blood pressure today is one thirty-six over eighty-two, and the pulse is seventy-eight. That's a reasonable pressure.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): One thirty-six I can live with. I get a bit wound up in the chair. I don't smoke, I never have, and the drink is two pints of a Saturday night, that's the height of it.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, the diabetes looks poorly controlled, with the thirst, the weight loss and the missed insulin. The tingling may be early nerve change in the feet. That's my working impression, and we'll let the bloods firm it up.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. What do you want me to do, then? I've a job on in the morning and I can't be losing days off the site.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm ordering an HbA1c and a urine ACR, the kidney check. The forms go with you today, so those are arranged, not maybe.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): And the eyes? I know I can't tell you the date, which is useless of me.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll refer you back to the diabetic eye screening. I want you back in this clinic in six weeks to go over the results and settle the insulin dose. Don't skip the Lantus even after an early shift, bring the glucose booklet in with you, and have a look at your feet every day. If a sore appears or the sight drops suddenly, ring us rather than waiting, and don't change the insulin number yourself.

[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks is grand, I'll be there. I'll bring the booklet from the van, and I won't be touching the dose if the letter and the pen still don't agree. Thanks a million, doctor.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

omissions.text: Insulin glargine/Lantus dose is documented incompletely: the patient said he injects 18 units nightly into the tummy, while an old nurse chart listed 24 units; the doctor explicitly said not to change the number and to leave the dose unchanged until the record is checked.

Insulin adherence detail missing: the patient said he skips the nightly Lantus about 3 nights a week, sometimes 4 if work runs on; weekends he never misses it, and some weeks he takes nearly all doses while some weeks only about half.

The recorded diabetic eye screening status is wrong/incomplete. The patient did not confirm a completed dated screening; he said he had eye screening at some point but could not say when, and the doctor planned to refer him back to diabetic eye screening.
Negative findings asked and answered but not recorded: no shaking and no sweating with suspected hypos.
Negative finding asked and answered but not recorded: no foot numbness.

omissions.text: Insulin glargine/Lantus dose per patient was stated as 18 units nightly, injected into the tummy; the medication entry lacks the patient-reported dose and route/site details.

The patient reported skipping his nightly Lantus on work days about three nights a week, and four if the job runs on; weekends he never misses it. This specific adherence pattern is clinically important and not captured in the medication record itself.
No known allergies was recorded, but the patient specifically said he has had penicillin before without any reaction.
The patient reported fasting glucose readings roughly 160-180+ and post-breakfast readings around 220 mg/dL, though he was uncertain of the exact values.

Negative finding omitted: no change in foot sensation was not true; initially denied pain/sores, but later clarified tingling in both toes at night for a few months. Any summary should reflect that numbness was asked about and not denied, because sensory symptoms were present.
Negative finding omitted: no burning on urination was recorded, but the patient also reported only getting up once at night to pass urine and attributed it to drinking a lot.
Negative finding omitted: no change in bowel habit was recorded, but the patient specifically said bowels were grand with no change at all.
